newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia looks to processed food for exports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia looks to processed food for exports.

text.p: Australian rural commodities exporters are looking to processed food exports to Asia for new growth as the farm sector faces flat forecast exports for traditional bulk produce.

Asian food consumption was growing by at least A$20 billion a year, Paul Bourke, executive director of Prime Minister John Howard's Supermarket to Asia Council, told the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) outlook conference on Tuesday.
Already more than half of Australia's food exports go to Asia but it accounts for only about six percent of food imports into the region, he said.
Australia's traditional strengths have been in bulk commodities, such as grains and minimally processed products including meat, sugar and dairy products.

But this year's ABARE conference painted a flat short-term picture for Australian rural exports, which are forecast to fall by 1.1 percent to A$20.2 billion in 1996/97 ending June 30 then to show zero growth in 1997/98.
"There's no doubt that the immediate outlook is not as bright as we'd like, it worries me immensely," John Anderson, Minister for Primary Industries and Energy, told reporters at the conference.

The Supermarket to Asia Council is made up of representatives of Australia's political, retailing, food, union, farmers, transport and packaging sectors and aims to boost Australian exports aimed for Asia's supermarket shelves.

Murray Rogers, chairman of the Australian Food Council, told the conference that the Asian market for food was estimated to grow by US$160 billion by 2000. Some estimates put the growth at $450 billion over the same period, he said.
Up to 90 percent of the extra demand would be for Asian food but the potential market growth for Western-style food might still be as high as US$16 billion, he said.
Other research indicated that the Southeast Asian food and agricultural products market alone could reach A$77 billion by 2010, he said.
"If Australia can maintain its market share of 7.5 percent ... the Australian food industry could increase its exports to Southeast Asia by almost A$5 billion by 2010," he said.
An increase of market share of only one percent a decade between now and 2010 would increase exports to A$7.7 billion, he said.
Total Australian processed food and beverage exports were about A$11 billion in 1995/96, most of it for Asia.
Anderson told the conference that the Supermarket to Asia thrust held the potential to make Australia a significant global supplier of food.
